items.label: text
items.text: Remember when an ionic compound dissolves in water, it splits into its ions.

items.label: text
items.text: Some reminders about oxidation and reduction:

items.label: text
items.text: reduction is gain of electrons An oxidising agent is something that oxidises something else by taking electrons away from it. Oxidising agents accept electrons and therefore are the things that are reduced in a reaction.

items.label: text
items.text: A reducing agent is something that reduces something else by giving electrons to it. Reducing agents give away electrons and therefore are the things that are oxidised in a reaction.

items.label: text
items.text: In all of the above reactions it would not have mattered if we had reacted chlorine with sodium bromide or magnesium bromide, for example. The reaction occurs between the chlorine molecule and the bromide ion; the metal ion does not do anything, we call it a spectator ion.If we write the reaction between chlorine and potassium iodide showing all the charges, we can see this more clearly:

items.text: You can see that the potassium ions are the same on each side. They have not changed and so we can write a new equation simply concentrating on the things that have changed:

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 B r ( a q ) + C I _ { 2 } ( a q ) \rightarrow 2 C I ( a q ) + B r _ { 2 } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: This is called an ionic equation and does not include the spectator ions.

items.label: text
items.text: The reactions above that do show a colour change are often discussed in terms of oxidation and reduction, they are redox reactions. If you have not already covered redox reactions, you should look at Chapter 14 before reading the next section.

items.label: text
items.text: If we look at the reaction between chlorine and either bromide ions or iodide ions, we can see why they are described as redox reactions.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 12.8 The reaction of chlorine with potassium bromide (top) or potassium iodide (below).

items.label: text
items.text: In each case, the chlorine is acting as an oxidising agent. In the first equation it oxidises the Br- ions by taking electrons away from them. Because the oxidising agent takes electrons away from something else, it is reduced itself: the Cl₂is reduced to 2Cl- ions.
